Aneuploidy is the correct answer. The term aneuploidy is derived from Greek meaning 'uneven number' (aneuno = not 2n). Aneuploidy is a change in the number of chromosomes that cannot be divided by the whole number n. This means that the number of chromosomes is not a multiple of the haploid number. For example, monosomy would be 2n-1 and trisomy would be 2n+1. Polyploidy is a change in the total chromosome number due to the multiplication of the entire set of chromosomes. For example triploidy would be 3n. Monosomy is a type of aneuploidy where one chromosome is missing from each of the two copies of a particular chromosome pair.

A reduced FEV1:FVC ratio is indicative of obstructive lung disease. Pulmonary fibrosis is an example of restrictive lung disease as the interstitium becomes scarred and thickened so less air can be inflated into the lungs. This means that the patient will exhale all the air in their lungs more quickly and therefore have a high FEV1:FVC ratio.  In obstructive lung disease, the airways become narrowed and it becomes harder to get the chest wall moving to inflate the lungs. This means that the patient will take longer to exhale all the air in their lungs and therefore have a reduced FEV1:FVC ratio.

Lynch Syndrome is associated with colorectal cancer, and has an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. It has been suggested that the reason for the early onset of cancer is that the mutation is germline, and therefore multiple generations are affected. The mutation in Lynch syndrome is in mismatch repair genes.  FAP (Familial Adenomatous Polyposis) is also inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, but is caused by a mutation in the APC gene. It is characterised by the development of hundreds of polyps in the colon, and eventually colorectal cancer.  MYH is a gene that codes for myosin II, and is associated with an autosomal dominant form of colorectal cancer called Lynch-like syndrome.  APC is a gene that is part of the Wnt signalling pathway. It is a scaffolding protein that helps to regulate the activity of β-catenin. When the APC protein is mutated, it is no longer able to regulate β-catenin, and so β-catenin accumulates in the cell. This leads to the transcription of genes that promote tumour growth.  Mismatch repair genes are a group of genes that code for proteins involved in the mismatch repair pathway. When these genes are mutated, the mismatch repair pathway is impaired, and so DNA replication is less accurate. This leads to the accumulation of mutations in cells, which may lead to cancer.

Sentinel cells are cells that reside in peripheral tissues, and act as the first line of defence against infection. They are called sentinels because they are the first cells to encounter a pathogen. They can be activated and then migrate to the nearest lymph node to present the pathogen's antigen to T cells. This allows the adaptive immune response to be mounted.  Natural killer cells are not considered sentinel cells, because they are not located in peripheral tissues, but are instead found in the blood. They are part of the innate immune system, and are important in the viral infection response. They kill target cells that have been infected by a virus, before the adaptive immune response has been mounted.

HCN4 channels are hyperpolarised cyclic gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels. Activation of beta adrenergic receptors via noradrenaline causes an increase in cAMP which activates PKA. PKA phosphorylates HCN4 channels causing them to open at rest. This causes an increase in the 'funny current' and therefore an increase in pacemaker slope. This means that the action potential reaches threshold quicker and therefore the heart beats faster. This is an increase in chronotropy. Ryanodine receptors are the receptors on the SR that are activated by increased Ca2+ movement into the cell. This causes more Ca2+ to be released from the SR which causes a stronger contraction. Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy is the most common type of diabetic neuropathy. It is characterised by a slow onset, symmetrical, length-dependent sensory and/or motor loss starting at the feet and progressing proximally. The loss of sensation is usually started by the soles of the feet and progresses to the toes, shins, knees, thighs, and eventually the upper leg. The rate of progression varies. Other types of diabetic neuropathy include autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathy and diabetic amyotrophy.Autonomic neuropathy is the most common form of diabetic autonomic neuropathy and is characterised by orthostatic hypotension, bladder dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, gastroparesis, and temperature dysregulation.Mononeuropathy is a term used for diabetic neuropathy that affects a single nerve. Diabetic amyotrophy is a painful, asymmetric, chronic neuropathy that primarily affects the proximal muscles of the hip and thigh. It is thought to be a form of chronic entrapment neuropathy. It usually affects older people and is more common in men. The pain is often severe and can lead to muscle wasting. It is thought to be due to a combination of factors, including chronic inflammation, nerve entrapment, and ischaemia.

Spinal stenosis: History is classically described as low back pain which is worse on walking particularly when going downhill. The pain is relieved by sitting down or leaning forward (which increases the diameter of the spinal canal). The pain is usually bilateral and accompanied by tingling. Straight leg raise is classically negative. Extension is usually limited and flexion may be painful.  Peripheral arterial disease: Pain is usually worse on walking up hills. The pain is relieved by stopping and standing. The pain is usually unilateral. Straight leg raise is classically negative.  Prolapsed IV disc: History is classically described as low back pain which is worse on walking particularly when going downhill. The pain is relieved by sitting down or leaning forward (which increases the diameter of the spinal canal). The pain is usually bilateral and accompanied by tingling. Straight leg raise is classically negative.  Chronic mechanical back pain: Pain is usually bilateral and accompanied by tingling. Straight leg raise is classically negative.  Metastatic spinal cord compression: History is classically described as low back pain which is worse at rest. The pain is relieved by walking. Agranulocytosis is a severe form of neutropenia characterised by a marked reduction in the absolute neutrophil count. It is an undesirable side effect of certain drugs, most commonly clozapine. Clozapine should not be used in patients with a history of agranulocytosis or neutropenia. Patients on clozapine should be monitored for signs of agranulocytosis, particularly during the initial 1-2 months of treatment. Regular blood monitoring is also recommended.
